label: Median time from ready to shipped
also_known_as: lead time for changes | cycle time | DORA lead time
plain_english: Once a developer says 'my change is ready', this is how long it typically waits before it becomes part of the product. Half of all changes are faster than this, half slower.
why_it_matters: This is the clearest single measure of how responsive engineering is to a request. A commitment made to a customer on Monday can only ship as fast as this number allows, and a long wait almost always means people are blocked on each other rather than working.
how_to_read: Under a day is strong. Several days means review has become a bottleneck. But a figure measured in minutes is also a warning, not a win: it usually means nobody is reviewing. Always read this next to review coverage.
formula: median(merged_at - created_at) over {n} merged pull requests = {value} hours
assumptions: A pull request counts as 'ready' the moment it is opened. Teams that open drafts early to share progress will look slower here than they really are.
caveats: Pull requests are fetched newest-first up to the configured page limit, so on very busy repositories the oldest pull requests can fall outside the collected window. The sample figures on this metric state exactly how many were read.

label: Slowest tenth of changes take at least
plain_english: Nine out of ten changes reach the product faster than this. The remaining one in ten takes at least this long. It describes the bad weeks rather than the typical day.
why_it_matters: Teams get judged on their worst delivery, not their median. This is the number a stakeholder remembers when something 'took forever', and it is where unclear ownership and stalled reviews actually show up.
how_to_read: Compare it against the median. If the slowest tenth takes ten times the median, the process is unpredictable even when the average looks healthy — and unpredictability is harder to plan around than slowness.
formula: 90th percentile(merged_at - created_at) over {n} merged pull requests = {value} hours
caveats: Pull requests are fetched newest-first up to the configured page limit, so on very busy repositories the oldest pull requests can fall outside the collected window. The sample figures on this metric state exactly how many were read.

label: Median wait for the first human review
plain_english: How long a finished change sits untouched before a colleague looks at it. This is pure waiting: the work is complete, and nothing is happening to it.
why_it_matters: This is usually the largest single removable delay in software delivery, and fixing it costs nothing but attention. It is also the part of the wait developers find most demoralising, precisely because the work is finished and idle.
how_to_read: Under four working hours is healthy. Over a day means reviewing is nobody's priority. 'Not available' means no reviews were recorded at all — which is itself the finding, and a more serious one than a slow number.
formula: median(first_review_at - created_at) over {n} reviewed pull requests = {value} hours
assumptions: Only reviews recorded through GitHub's review feature count. Approval given in a plain comment, over chat, or in person is invisible to this metric.
caveats: Pull requests are fetched newest-first up to the configured page limit, so on very busy repositories the oldest pull requests can fall outside the collected window. The sample figures on this metric state exactly how many were read.

label: Releases to the main branch per week
plain_english: How many separate times each week finished work lands on the branch the product is built from. Roughly: how often this team ships.
why_it_matters: Shipping in small, frequent pieces is the most consistently reproduced predictor of both speed and stability in the research literature. Rare large releases concentrate risk into stressful events that people learn to fear and therefore delay further.
how_to_read: Daily or better is elite. Weekly is solid. Less than monthly usually means releasing is a manual event rather than a routine one.
formula: {landings} landings on {branch} over {weeks} weeks = {value} per week
assumptions: Each merge or direct push to the default branch counts as one landing, because no deployment system is connected to this tool.
caveats: With no deployment system feeding this tool, a landing on the default branch stands in for a release. A team that batches merges and releases weekly will be over-counted here.

label: Share of changes that needed a fix or revert
plain_english: Out of every hundred changes that shipped, roughly how many had to be undone or urgently patched afterwards.
why_it_matters: Speed only counts if the work stays shipped. A rising value means the team is paying for its velocity in rework, and that bill usually lands on whoever is on call.
how_to_read: Under 15% is the industry's 'good' band. Treat the exact figure with real caution: it is inferred from how people word their commits, so a team that never writes 'fix' will look artificially healthy and a disciplined team will look worse than it is.
formula: {failures} remediation commits / {landings} landings = {value}%
assumptions: A commit counts as remediation when git records it as a revert, or when its subject line opens with a hotfix or revert marker.
caveats: This reads commit messages, not incidents. It is a conversation starter, not a reliability measurement. Connecting an incident tracker is what turns it into one. | A team that writes 'fix:' on ordinary small corrections scores worse than a team that writes nothing at all, which is the opposite of the truth.

label: Median time to repair a reverted change
plain_english: When something had to be undone, this is how long the broken version stayed in place before the correction landed.
why_it_matters: Everything breaks eventually; what separates teams is how fast they recover. Short recovery means problems get contained before customers accumulate.
how_to_read: Under an hour is elite. Over a day suggests either detection or the release path is slow. Check the sample size first — most repositories have only a handful of events, so one outlier moves this a long way.
formula: median(revert_time - original_commit_time) over {n} revert pairs = {value} hours
assumptions: Only reverts where git recorded the original commit hash can be paired and timed.
caveats: Measures time to revert in source control, not time to restore service for customers. Those two differ by however long the release path takes. | Usually computed over very few events, so read it as an anecdote with a number attached.

label: Changes currently waiting
also_known_as: work in progress | WIP | open PR queue
plain_english: How many finished-but-not-yet-shipped changes are sitting open right now, waiting for review or a decision.
why_it_matters: This is inventory. Every open change is effort already spent that has not yet produced any value, and it decays: the longer it waits, the more it conflicts with other work and the more expensive it becomes to finish.
how_to_read: Roughly one open change per active developer is normal. Several times that means the team is starting faster than it can finish, and adding more work will not help.
formula: count(pull requests open at collection time) = {value}
caveats: Pull requests are fetched newest-first up to the configured page limit, so on very busy repositories the oldest pull requests can fall outside the collected window. The sample figures on this metric state exactly how many were read.

label: Share of open changes stalled over 30 days
plain_english: Of the changes currently waiting, how many have had no activity at all for more than a month. In practice, work that was finished and then quietly forgotten.
why_it_matters: Each one is fully paid-for engineering effort delivering nothing. They also mislead planning, because the work looks 'in progress' when it is actually abandoned.
how_to_read: Under 10% is normal churn. Above a third means the review queue is not being worked, and the honest move is to close them rather than let them imply progress.
formula: {stale} open pull requests idle over 30 days / {open} open = {value}%
caveats: Pull requests are fetched newest-first up to the configured page limit, so on very busy repositories the oldest pull requests can fall outside the collected window. The sample figures on this metric state exactly how many were read.

label: Commits
plain_english: A commit is one saved checkpoint of work, like a numbered draft of a document. This is how many such checkpoints were recorded in the period.
why_it_matters: It is the raw pulse of activity and the denominator for most percentages on this page. On its own it says nothing at all about value delivered.
how_to_read: Use it for shape and trend, never as a target. Teams differ tenfold in how finely they slice their work, and both extremes can be perfectly healthy.
formula: count(commits in scope, merge commits excluded) = {value}
assumptions: Merge commits are excluded, because they restate the line changes of the commits they bring in and would double-count every line.
caveats: If the team squash-merges pull requests, many individual commits collapse into one. Per-commit counts are then lower than the work actually done, and individual authorship inside a squashed change is lost entirely. | Rebases, force-pushes and history rewrites change commit hashes and dates. Older history can therefore appear tidier, or more recent, than it actually was.

label: Lines of code added
plain_english: How many individual lines of code were written in the period, after removing machine-generated and third-party files that nobody actually typed.
why_it_matters: It gives a sense of scale — a thousand-line month and a hundred-thousand-line month are very different situations — and it is the denominator for the test ratio and the AI line share.
how_to_read: Treat large spikes as questions rather than achievements. The usual explanations are an initial code import, a dependency upgrade, or a file type the exclusion rules missed.
formula: sum(added lines over {files} counted files) = {value}
caveats: Generated, vendored, minified and dependency-lock files are excluded from line counts by the rules in config/path_rules.yaml. Anything those rules miss will inflate line totals, so check the excluded-file report before quoting a large number. | Lines of code measures volume, not value. A hard-won hundred-line fix and a thousand lines of boilerplate look the same here. This is not a basis for ranking people.

label: Lines of code removed
plain_english: How many lines of code were deleted during the period. Deleting code is a normal and usually welcome part of the work: it happens when something is replaced by a simpler version, when a feature is retired, or when a mistake is undone.
why_it_matters: Deletion is usually a good sign: it means simplification and cleanup are happening rather than only accumulation. A codebase that only ever grows steadily gets harder and more expensive to change.
how_to_read: Compare against lines added. Roughly balanced means the team is reworking what exists; heavily additive means new construction.
formula: sum(removed lines over {files} counted files) = {value}
caveats: Generated, vendored, minified and dependency-lock files are excluded from line counts by the rules in config/path_rules.yaml. Anything those rules miss will inflate line totals, so check the excluded-file report before quoting a large number. | Lines of code measures volume, not value. A hard-won hundred-line fix and a thousand lines of boilerplate look the same here. This is not a basis for ranking people.

label: Net change in codebase size
plain_english: Lines added minus lines removed — how much bigger or smaller the codebase got overall.
why_it_matters: Size is the main driver of long-term maintenance cost. Watching net growth against delivered features tells you whether the team is building capability or accumulating bulk.
how_to_read: Steady modest growth is normal for an active product. A negative figure during an active period is usually a successful cleanup and worth celebrating rather than questioning.
formula: {added} added - {removed} removed = {value} net lines
caveats: Generated, vendored, minified and dependency-lock files are excluded from line counts by the rules in config/path_rules.yaml. Anything those rules miss will inflate line totals, so check the excluded-file report before quoting a large number. | Lines of code measures volume, not value. A hard-won hundred-line fix and a thousand lines of boilerplate look the same here. This is not a basis for ranking people.

label: Days per week with any activity
plain_english: On how many days in a typical week does anyone save work to this codebase. It separates steady daily progress from occasional bursts.
why_it_matters: A steady cadence usually indicates well-understood work flowing smoothly. Long silences followed by bursts normally mean work is blocked elsewhere, or being done privately on a branch and landed in one go.
how_to_read: Four to five is normal for an actively staffed team. One or two means the project is in maintenance, or a single person is carrying it.
formula: {active_days} distinct active days / {weeks} weeks = {value} days per week
caveats: Rebases, force-pushes and history rewrites change commit hashes and dates. Older history can therefore appear tidier, or more recent, than it actually was.

label: Median commit size
plain_english: The size of a typical saved checkpoint, counting lines added and removed together.
why_it_matters: Small commits are easier to review, easier to undo, and far easier to understand a year later when something breaks. Very large commits cannot be reviewed meaningfully at all.
how_to_read: Tens of lines is comfortable. Hundreds means changes are hard to review. A sudden rise alongside rising AI adoption is worth investigating rather than celebrating.
formula: median(added + removed per commit) over {n} commits = {value} lines
caveats: Generated, vendored, minified and dependency-lock files are excluded from line counts by the rules in config/path_rules.yaml. Anything those rules miss will inflate line totals, so check the excluded-file report before quoting a large number. | If the team squash-merges pull requests, many individual commits collapse into one. Per-commit counts are then lower than the work actually done, and individual authorship inside a squashed change is lost entirely.

label: Lines changed per active day
plain_english: On the days when work actually happened, how many lines of code changed on average.
why_it_matters: It normalises output for how many days the team was actually engaged, which makes two periods comparable even when one contains holidays or a hiring gap.
how_to_read: Only meaningful compared against the same codebase's own history. A step change that coincides with a tool rollout is the pattern worth examining.
formula: {lines} lines changed / {active_days} active days = {value} lines per active day
caveats: Generated, vendored, minified and dependency-lock files are excluded from line counts by the rules in config/path_rules.yaml. Anything those rules miss will inflate line totals, so check the excluded-file report before quoting a large number. | Lines of code measures volume, not value. A hard-won hundred-line fix and a thousand lines of boilerplate look the same here. This is not a basis for ranking people.

label: Share of work that is new capability
also_known_as: work composition | investment mix | feature vs maintenance
plain_english: Developers usually label what a change is for — new capability, a bug fix, a cleanup, or routine maintenance. This is the share of work labelled as new capability.
why_it_matters: This is the closest available answer to 'what are we actually spending engineering on?'. A quarter where most effort went to fixes and cleanup rather than new capability explains a missed roadmap far better than any velocity chart.
how_to_read: There is no correct number. Around half on new capability is common for a growing product; much lower means the team is absorbed by maintenance. Look for the trend, and check the coverage figure — this only works where teams label their commits.
formula: {feature} feature commits / {classified} classified commits = {value}%
assumptions: Classification reads conventional-commit prefixes (feat, fix, refactor, chore, docs, test, perf, ci, build, style) and falls back to keyword matching on the subject line.
caveats: Only commits that follow a recognisable convention can be classified. The coverage figure on this metric states what share of commits it could read at all — if that is low, the percentage describes a minority of the work. | Labels are self-reported. A change labelled 'refactor' that adds a feature is counted as a refactor.

label: Share of commits that are trivial
plain_english: The share of saved checkpoints that changed almost nothing — fewer than five lines, or only configuration and formatting.
why_it_matters: It stops commit counts being read as productivity. If a large share of a team's commits are one-line tweaks, then a rising commit count is a change in habit, not in output.
how_to_read: Twenty to thirty percent is normal, since real work includes small corrections. Much higher means commit counts are not a usable measure of anything for this team.
formula: {trivial} commits under {threshold} lines / {n} commits = {value}%
caveats: A one-line change can be the most important fix of the quarter. This measures size, which is not the same as significance. | Generated, vendored, minified and dependency-lock files are excluded from line counts by the rules in config/path_rules.yaml. Anything those rules miss will inflate line totals, so check the excluded-file report before quoting a large number.

label: Rework rate: new code rewritten within 21 days
also_known_as: churn rate | code churn | rework | thrash
plain_english: Of all the code written in this period, this share was changed again or deleted within three weeks of being written. Put plainly: work that did not stay put. Getting a requirement wrong and then correcting it lands here.
why_it_matters: This is the closest thing available to a measure of wasted effort. Every point of rework is engineering time spent twice on the same outcome. It is also usually caused upstream — unclear requirements, missing review, changing minds — rather than by careless coding, which makes it a management lever rather than a developer scorecard.
how_to_read: Under 15% is normal and healthy; some rework always happens and a codebase with none is probably not being maintained. Sustained above roughly 25% signals that work is starting before it is properly understood. A step up immediately after a tool rollout or a team change is the specific pattern worth investigating.
formula: {reworked_lines} lines rewritten within {window_days} days / {added_lines} lines added = {value}%
assumptions: A file touched again within 21 days is treated as rework in proportion to the lines changed on the second visit. This is file-level attribution, not line-level blame, which is the practical trade-off that keeps this affordable over years of history. | The 21-day window follows the convention used in the published code-churn research. It is a considered judgement, not a law of nature, and is configurable.
caveats: Legitimate iteration also lands here. A feature built across several days of successive commits looks like rework even though it is ordinary progress. | Generated, vendored, minified and dependency-lock files are excluded from line counts by the rules in config/path_rules.yaml. Anything those rules miss will inflate line totals, so check the excluded-file report before quoting a large number.

label: Share of new code that is tests
plain_english: Of every hundred lines of code written, how many were automated tests — code whose only job is to check that the rest of the code still works.
why_it_matters: Tests are how a team keeps moving quickly without breaking what already works. If output rises while this ratio falls, the team is borrowing speed from future stability, and that debt is repaid as production incidents at the least convenient moment.
how_to_read: Twenty to forty percent is typical for a well-tested service. Near zero on a codebase that is actively changing is the strongest early warning signal in this whole report.
formula: {test_lines} lines in test files / {total_lines} total lines added = {value}%
assumptions: A file counts as a test when its path matches a test directory or a test/spec naming convention. Language-specific layouts are configured in config/path_rules.yaml.
caveats: This counts the volume of test code, not whether the tests are any good or what they actually exercise. A thousand lines of shallow tests score better than a hundred excellent ones. | Generated, vendored, minified and dependency-lock files are excluded from line counts by the rules in config/path_rules.yaml. Anything those rules miss will inflate line totals, so check the excluded-file report before quoting a large number.

label: Share of code changes that updated tests too
plain_english: When a developer changed real product code, how often did they change a test in the same checkpoint. It measures whether testing happens alongside the work or gets deferred.
why_it_matters: A team can have a healthy overall test ratio while still shipping most individual changes untested, if tests arrive in occasional big batches. This catches that pattern, which the overall ratio hides.
how_to_read: Above 40% is a strong habit. Below 15% means tests are an afterthought, regardless of what the total test ratio says.
formula: {coupled} commits touching both code and tests / {code_commits} code commits = {value}%
caveats: Not every code change needs a test change — a rename or a config tweak legitimately does not. This will therefore never reach 100%, and should not. | Generated, vendored, minified and dependency-lock files are excluded from line counts by the rules in config/path_rules.yaml. Anything those rules miss will inflate line totals, so check the excluded-file report before quoting a large number.

label: Share of all changes landing in the busiest 10 files
plain_english: Out of all the editing that happened, this share happened inside just ten files. It shows whether work is spread across the codebase or piling up in a few crowded places.
why_it_matters: Files that every change touches are where merge conflicts, regressions and onboarding pain concentrate. They are also the highest-return refactoring targets in the codebase, because one well-chosen split relieves pressure on every future change.
how_to_read: Under 20% means change is well distributed. Over 40% means a handful of files are acting as a bottleneck for the whole team. The named files are listed underneath as evidence, so this metric comes with its own to-do list.
formula: changes in top {top_n} files ({top_changes}) / all file changes ({all_changes}) = {value}%
caveats: Generated, vendored, minified and dependency-lock files are excluded from line counts by the rules in config/path_rules.yaml. Anything those rules miss will inflate line totals, so check the excluded-file report before quoting a large number.

label: Share of changes too large to review properly
plain_english: The share of proposed changes bigger than 400 lines — the size past which review research consistently shows reviewers stop finding defects and start skimming.
why_it_matters: A large change that gets approved has not really been reviewed. This measures how much of the review process is ceremony, which matters most precisely when delivery is fastest.
how_to_read: Under 20% is healthy. A high value combined with a very fast median merge time is strong evidence that changes are being waved through rather than examined.
formula: {large} pull requests over {threshold} lines / {n} pull requests = {value}%
assumptions: The 400-line threshold comes from published code-review research; it is a convention rather than a property of your codebase.
caveats: Pull requests are fetched newest-first up to the configured page limit, so on very busy repositories the oldest pull requests can fall outside the collected window. The sample figures on this metric state exactly how many were read. | Generated, vendored, minified and dependency-lock files are excluded from line counts by the rules in config/path_rules.yaml. Anything those rules miss will inflate line totals, so check the excluded-file report before quoting a large number.

label: Share of functions long enough to be hard to follow
plain_english: Code is organised into functions — named blocks that each do one job. This is the share of them longer than 60 lines, which is roughly the point where a reader can no longer hold the whole thing in their head at once.
why_it_matters: Long functions are where bugs hide and where new joiners stall. They are also the most commonly reported side effect of generated code, since a tool asked for a working solution will happily produce one long block rather than several well-named small ones.
how_to_read: Under 10% is tidy. Over 25% means the codebase is structurally difficult to work in, and onboarding time will reflect that. Watch the trend more than the level.
formula: {long} functions over {threshold} lines / {n} functions found = {value}%
caveats: Structure is measured with a brace-and-indent scanner, not a full language parser. It is reliable for ordinary code and can be fooled by macros, generated code, and unusual formatting. Treat the trend as the signal and any single file as a lead to verify. | Some languages and frameworks legitimately produce long declarative blocks — configuration, schema definitions, generated builders — which inflate this.

label: Deepest nesting in the worst tenth of functions
plain_english: How deeply conditions and loops sit inside one another — an 'if' inside a loop inside another 'if' is depth three. Deeper means more paths through the code and more ways for it to go wrong.
why_it_matters: Nesting depth predicts defect rates better than raw size does, and it is the property that makes code genuinely hard to reason about rather than merely long.
how_to_read: Three or four is ordinary. Six or more in the worst tenth means there are functions in this codebase that nobody can safely change without tests.
formula: 90th percentile(max nesting depth per function) over {n} functions = {value}
caveats: Structure is measured with a brace-and-indent scanner, not a full language parser. It is reliable for ordinary code and can be fooled by macros, generated code, and unusual formatting. Treat the trend as the signal and any single file as a lead to verify.

label: Share of code that is copy-pasted
also_known_as: code duplication | clone rate | copy-paste detection
plain_english: The share of lines that appear as part of a repeated block found somewhere else in the codebase — the same six or more lines written twice.
why_it_matters: Duplication multiplies the cost of every future fix: a bug in a copied block has to be found and fixed in each copy, and the copies drift apart over time. It is also the most frequently observed consequence of generating code rather than reusing it.
how_to_read: Under 5% is normal. Over 15% means fixes are systematically incomplete, and the trend matters more than the level. Test files legitimately repeat setup code, so check whether the duplication is in tests or in product code.
formula: {duplicated_lines} lines inside repeated {window}-line blocks / {scanned_lines} scanned = {value}%
assumptions: Blocks are compared after normalising whitespace and stripping comments, using a sliding window of 6 lines. Exact-match detection only — near-duplicates with renamed variables are not caught, so this is a floor.
caveats: Generated, vendored, minified and dependency-lock files are excluded from line counts by the rules in config/path_rules.yaml. Anything those rules miss will inflate line totals, so check the excluded-file report before quoting a large number. | Detects identical blocks only. Real-world duplication with renamed variables is invisible here, so the true figure is higher than reported.

label: Share of lines that are comments
plain_english: How much of the code is explanatory notes written for humans rather than instructions for the computer.
why_it_matters: Comments carry the reasoning that code cannot express — why a decision was made, what was tried and rejected. That reasoning is what a new joiner or a future maintainer actually needs, and it is the first thing lost when code is generated rather than written.
how_to_read: Ten to twenty percent is typical. Very low means intent lives only in people's heads. Very high can mean boilerplate documentation headers that say nothing. Read the trend, not the level.
formula: {comment_lines} comment lines / {scanned_lines} scanned lines = {value}%
caveats: Structure is measured with a brace-and-indent scanner, not a full language parser. It is reliable for ordinary code and can be fooled by macros, generated code, and unusual formatting. Treat the trend as the signal and any single file as a lead to verify. | Comment volume is not comment quality. Generated documentation headers count the same as a hard-won explanation of a subtle bug.

label: Commits carrying an AI-tool trace (floor)
also_known_as: AI adoption | AI-assisted commit share | AI %
plain_english: Some AI coding tools leave a small signature in the record of a change, rather like a photocopier leaving a faint mark. This is the share of changes carrying such a signature. It can only count the ones that left a mark, so the real figure is higher — how much higher is genuinely unknown.
why_it_matters: It is the only retrospective evidence of AI adoption that exists across full history, and the floor alone is often decisive for a licensing conversation: if the floor is already high, the tools are clearly in use whatever the true number is.
how_to_read: Read it aloud as 'at least this much', never as 'this much'. A rising floor over time is meaningful. The absolute level is not comparable between teams, because it depends on which tools they chose and whether they left the default settings alone.
formula: {detected} commits with an AI trace / {n} commits = {value}%
assumptions: Detection patterns live in config/ai_signatures.yaml and cover commit trailers and message fingerprints from Claude Code, GitHub Copilot, Cursor, Aider, Windsurf, Devin and any custom 'AI-Assisted:' trailer the organisation chooses to mandate.
caveats: This is a floor, not a measurement. It counts only work where a tool chose to leave a trace in commit metadata, and every one of those traces can be switched off in a single setting. | Nothing here says AI wrote the code. It says an AI tool was involved in producing the change. A developer who accepted a single suggestion and one who generated an entire file are indistinguishable in this data. | Tool-native analytics (Cursor, Copilot) only report from the day telemetry was enabled. History before that point was never recorded and cannot be reconstructed after the fact.

label: Lines arriving in AI-traced commits (floor)
plain_english: The share of all code lines that arrived inside a change carrying an AI signature. Note the careful wording: lines that came in alongside an AI trace, not lines an AI wrote.
why_it_matters: It converts adoption into something closer to volume, which is what people actually mean when they ask 'how much of our code is AI'. Giving them this number with its wording intact is more useful than refusing to answer.
how_to_read: Always higher than nothing and always lower than the truth. Use it to compare periods within one team. Do not use it to compare teams, and do not let it be quoted as 'the percentage of our code that is AI'.
formula: {detected_lines} lines in AI-traced commits / {total_lines} lines = {value}%
caveats: This is a floor, not a measurement. It counts only work where a tool chose to leave a trace in commit metadata, and every one of those traces can be switched off in a single setting. | A commit mixing hand-written and AI-assisted code attributes all of its lines to the AI side. That overstates within the commits it catches, while the overall figure understates. The two errors do not reliably cancel out. | Generated, vendored, minified and dependency-lock files are excluded from line counts by the rules in config/path_rules.yaml. Anything those rules miss will inflate line totals, so check the excluded-file report before quoting a large number.

label: Contributors with any AI-traced commit
plain_english: The share of people contributing to this code who have at least one change carrying an AI signature. It measures how widely the tools have spread, not how heavily they are used.
why_it_matters: Breadth and depth of adoption call for completely different responses. A few power users means the opportunity is training and enablement. Broad shallow use means the opportunity is workflow and integration.
how_to_read: Compare it against how many licences were issued. A large gap between seats paid for and people showing any trace is the single most actionable number in this family, because it converts directly into either a training plan or a cancelled renewal.
formula: {adopters} contributors with an AI trace / {n} contributors = {value}%
caveats: This is a floor, not a measurement. It counts only work where a tool chose to leave a trace in commit metadata, and every one of those traces can be switched off in a single setting. | Anyone who disabled their tool's commit trailer appears here as a non-adopter, so this understates adoption in exactly the population most comfortable changing settings.

label: Share of AI traces from the single most-used tool
plain_english: Of all the AI signatures found, this share came from one tool. It shows whether the organisation has settled on a standard or has several tools in parallel use.
why_it_matters: Tool sprawl costs money in duplicate licences and costs more in fragmented practice — prompts, conventions and lessons do not transfer between tools. It also tells you which vendor relationship actually matters at renewal time.
how_to_read: Near 100% means one tool dominates, which simplifies both purchasing and enablement. A spread across three or more suggests adoption happened bottom-up without a decision.
formula: {top_tool_commits} traces from {top_tool} / {total_traces} traces = {value}%
caveats: This is a floor, not a measurement. It counts only work where a tool chose to leave a trace in commit metadata, and every one of those traces can be switched off in a single setting. | Tools differ enormously in how readily they leave a trace, so this reflects trace-leaving behaviour at least as much as actual usage. A quiet tool looks unused.

label: Rework gap between AI-traced and untraced work
plain_english: Whether code arriving with an AI signature gets rewritten more or less often than the rest. A positive number means AI-traced work needed more revisiting than other work.
why_it_matters: It is the most direct available answer to 'is AI-assisted code holding up?'. If speed arrives with a rework penalty, the net productivity gain is smaller than the velocity chart implies, and that is exactly the arithmetic a leadership team needs.
how_to_read: Treat anything within a few percentage points as noise. Look for a consistent gap that persists across several quarters, then confirm it on one specific repository with named examples before acting on it.
formula: rework in AI-traced ({ai_rate}%) - rework in untraced ({human_rate}%) = {value} points
caveats: This is a correlation between two rough proxies, not a causal finding. The people using AI tools most heavily are often also working on the least familiar code, which on its own would produce this gap. | The AI-assisted side of this comparison is only the work where a tool left a trace in commit metadata, and any developer can switch that trace off. The cohort is therefore smaller than the real one, which widens the uncertainty on this difference in both directions.

label: Test-ratio gap between AI-traced and untraced work
plain_english: Whether changes carrying an AI signature include proportionally more or fewer tests than other changes. A negative number means AI-traced work came with fewer tests.
why_it_matters: AI tools are demonstrably good at writing tests when asked. If this gap is negative, the problem is workflow rather than capability — people are not asking — and that is a cheap fix with a large payoff.
how_to_read: A positive gap is a genuinely good sign worth publicising internally. A strongly negative gap alongside high AI adoption is the clearest 'act now' combination in this report.
formula: test ratio in AI-traced ({ai_rate}%) - in untraced ({human_rate}%) = {value} points
caveats: The AI-assisted side of this comparison is only the work where a tool left a trace in commit metadata, and any developer can switch that trace off. The cohort is therefore smaller than the real one, which widens the uncertainty on this difference in both directions. | Confounded by the kind of work people choose AI for. Exploratory work legitimately carries fewer tests regardless of how it was written.

label: Size gap between AI-traced and untraced commits
plain_english: Whether changes carrying an AI signature tend to be bigger or smaller than other changes, expressed as a percentage difference in typical size.
why_it_matters: Larger changes are harder to review, so if AI-assisted work is systematically bigger then AI adoption quietly increases review burden. That cost usually lands on senior engineers and is rarely accounted for in the productivity case.
how_to_read: A large positive number means review capacity needs to grow alongside AI adoption. Combine with review coverage to see whether it already failed to.
formula: median AI-traced size ({ai_size}) vs untraced ({human_size}) = {value}% difference
caveats: The AI-assisted side of this comparison is only the work where a tool left a trace in commit metadata, and any developer can switch that trace off. The cohort is therefore smaller than the real one, which widens the uncertainty on this difference in both directions. | Generated, vendored, minified and dependency-lock files are excluded from line counts by the rules in config/path_rules.yaml. Anything those rules miss will inflate line totals, so check the excluded-file report before quoting a large number.

label: AI tool configuration files present
plain_english: AI coding tools often keep a settings or instructions file in the repository — files named CLAUDE.md, .cursorrules, copilot-instructions.md and similar. This counts how many are present.
why_it_matters: Unlike commit traces, these files cannot be switched off without deleting them, so they are an independent corroborating signal. A repository with a tool config file and a zero commit-trace rate is strong evidence that traces are being suppressed rather than that the tool is unused.
how_to_read: Presence proves a tool was deliberately set up for this repository. Absence proves nothing, since most usage needs no configuration file at all.
formula: count(files matching known AI tool config patterns) = {value}
assumptions: Patterns are listed in config/ai_signatures.yaml under artifact_files and are matched against the current checkout of the default branch only.

label: Active contributors
plain_english: How many distinct people saved work to this codebase during the period, after merging the several email addresses one person often uses and removing automated accounts.
why_it_matters: This is the real staffing level, as opposed to the planned one. Comparing it against the team roster frequently reveals that fewer people are actually in the code than anyone believed, which reframes a delivery conversation immediately.
how_to_read: Compare against the roster for this project. Persistently lower means the plan and the reality have diverged, and the plan is the thing that is wrong.
formula: count(distinct human contributors after identity merge) = {value}
assumptions: Identities are merged by email address first, then by normalised display name, using any explicit alias rules in config/identities.yaml. Bot accounts are excluded by pattern.
caveats: Pair and ensemble programming credit a single author for several people's work. | If the team squash-merges pull requests, many individual commits collapse into one. Per-commit counts are then lower than the work actually done, and individual authorship inside a squashed change is lost entirely.

label: Bus factor: people holding half the code
also_known_as: key person risk | knowledge concentration | truck factor
plain_english: The smallest number of people who between them wrote half of all the code here. If that number is one, then a single person's departure — or holiday — takes half the working knowledge of this codebase with them.
why_it_matters: It is a staffing risk expressed as a single number, and it is the metric most likely to change a hiring, documentation or pairing decision. Unlike most risks in this report it is cheap to fix once you know precisely where it sits.
how_to_read: One or two is a genuine risk worth acting on this quarter. Three or more on a small team is reasonable. Read it alongside the contributor list: a bus factor of one on a one-person prototype is expected, not alarming.
formula: smallest k where the top k contributors exceed 50% of {total_lines} lines = {value}
assumptions: Lines written stands in for knowledge held. Reviewers and architects who shaped the code without typing much of it are invisible to this measure, so it understates resilience on teams with strong review cultures.
caveats: Lines of code measures volume, not value. A hard-won hundred-line fix and a thousand lines of boilerplate look the same here. This is not a basis for ranking people. | If the team squash-merges pull requests, many individual commits collapse into one. Per-commit counts are then lower than the work actually done, and individual authorship inside a squashed change is lost entirely.

label: Share of the code written by one person
plain_english: How much of all the code in this period came from the single most prolific contributor.
why_it_matters: It is the bus factor with the detail restored. A single person at 70% is a different conversation from three people at 25% each, even though both can produce the same bus factor, and the mitigation differs too.
how_to_read: Above 50% on a team of several people means the work is not really shared, whatever the org chart says. On a solo project it is simply a fact rather than a finding.
formula: {top_lines} lines from {top_name} / {total_lines} total lines = {value}%
caveats: Lines of code measures volume, not value. A hard-won hundred-line fix and a thousand lines of boilerplate look the same here. This is not a basis for ranking people. | This breaks down by individual. Published research and hard experience both show that per-person delivery metrics change behaviour once people can see themselves ranked. Use it to find where help is needed, not to compare colleagues.

label: Share of work from people new to this codebase
plain_english: How much of the work in this period came from people whose very first change to this codebase was less than 90 days ago.
why_it_matters: Newcomer-heavy periods need more review capacity and reliably produce more rework. That is normal and temporary. Knowing the share explains a quality dip factually, without anyone having to be blamed for it.
how_to_read: High values on a deliberately growing team are expected and fine. High values on a team that is supposed to be stable point at turnover worth understanding.
formula: {newcomer_lines} lines from contributors under 90 days / {total_lines} lines = {value}%
caveats: This measures tenure on this repository, not at the company. A twenty-year veteran joining a new project counts as a newcomer — which is the right reading for review load, and the wrong one for seniority.

label: Share of files only one person has ever touched
also_known_as: knowledge silo | single-owner files | orphan risk
plain_english: The share of code files that exactly one person has ever edited. Nobody else has seen them closely enough to have changed anything in them.
why_it_matters: This is the bus factor at file resolution, which makes it actionable: it produces an actual list of files needing a second reader. It is also where incidents become long incidents, because the only person who understands the code may be asleep.
how_to_read: Some single-owner files are inevitable and harmless. Above 50% means the codebase is a collection of private territories rather than shared property, and reviewing will not fix it on its own — deliberate pairing will.
formula: {single_owner} files with exactly one distinct author / {files} files = {value}%
assumptions: Authorship comes from commit history within the collected window. A file written years ago by someone who has left, and untouched since, counts as single-owner.
caveats: Generated and configuration files inflate this, since one person typically sets them up and nobody needs to return to them.

label: Share of contributors still active in the last 90 days
plain_english: Of everyone who has ever contributed to this codebase in the collected period, the share who were still contributing within the last three months.
why_it_matters: It distinguishes a codebase with a living team from one being maintained by whoever is left. A low figure means most of the knowledge about this code now sits with people who have moved on.
how_to_read: On a long-lived repository this is naturally low and not alarming. On a repository under active development, a low figure means the team turned over and the remaining people are working in code they did not write.
formula: {recent} contributors active in last 90 days / {total} contributors = {value}%
caveats: Someone who moved to another project deliberately looks identical to someone who left the company. This measures presence in this codebase, nothing more.

label: Share of merged changes with a recorded review
plain_english: Of the changes that went into the product through a pull request, how many had at least one colleague formally look at them and record an opinion.
why_it_matters: Review is the main defect-catching and knowledge-sharing mechanism most teams have. If coverage is low then a fast delivery time is not efficiency — it is an unguarded path to production, and every other process number here should be read in that light.
how_to_read: Above 90% is the expectation for shared code. Near zero means the pull request process exists on paper only. This is the metric to check before believing any good news in the delivery family.
formula: {reviewed} merged pull requests with a review / {merged} merged = {value}%
assumptions: Only GitHub review records count. Approval given in a plain comment, over chat, or in person is invisible, so a team with a different review habit will score unfairly low — verify against the listed examples before treating a low number as a finding.
caveats: Pull requests are fetched newest-first up to the configured page limit, so on very busy repositories the oldest pull requests can fall outside the collected window. The sample figures on this metric state exactly how many were read.

label: Share of changes merged by their own author
plain_english: How often the person who wrote a change was also the person who pressed the button to put it into the product, with nobody else involved in between.
why_it_matters: Self-merging is the specific mechanism by which a review policy quietly stops applying. It is also the first control weakness an auditor asks about in regulated work, and the easiest to fix — it is a branch-protection setting.
how_to_read: Some self-merging is fine on small internal tools. Consistently high values on a customer-facing codebase is a governance finding, not a style preference.
formula: {self_merged} pull requests merged by their author / {merged} merged = {value}%
caveats: Pull requests are fetched newest-first up to the configured page limit, so on very busy repositories the oldest pull requests can fall outside the collected window. The sample figures on this metric state exactly how many were read. | A change properly reviewed and approved by a colleague and then merged by its author still counts here. Read this next to review coverage rather than alone.

label: Median change size
plain_english: The size of a typical proposed change, counting lines added and removed together.
why_it_matters: Size is the strongest single predictor of whether a review will find anything. Small changes get real scrutiny; large ones get approved.
how_to_read: Under 200 lines is reviewable. Over 500 means review quality is compromised.
formula: median(additions + deletions) over {n} pull requests = {value} lines
caveats: Pull requests are fetched newest-first up to the configured page limit, so on very busy repositories the oldest pull requests can fall outside the collected window. The sample figures on this metric state exactly how many were read. | Generated, vendored, minified and dependency-lock files are excluded from line counts by the rules in config/path_rules.yaml. Anything those rules miss will inflate line totals, so check the excluded-file report before quoting a large number.

label: Share of reviews done by one person
plain_english: Of all the reviews recorded, this share was done by a single person — the one doing the most reviewing.
why_it_matters: A single overloaded reviewer is both a delivery bottleneck and a burnout risk, and the cost is invisible in every other metric because their own output looks low while they unblock everyone else. This is the number that makes that work visible.
how_to_read: On a team of five, anything above 50% means one person is carrying review. Combine with the review-wait metric: if both are high, that one person is the constraint on the whole team's delivery.
formula: {top_reviews} reviews by {top_reviewer} / {total_reviews} reviews = {value}%
caveats: Pull requests are fetched newest-first up to the configured page limit, so on very busy repositories the oldest pull requests can fall outside the collected window. The sample figures on this metric state exactly how many were read. | Counts review events, not review effort. A one-word approval and a detailed critique count the same.

label: Share of work that bypassed pull requests
plain_english: How much work reached the main branch without going through the pull request process at all — pushed straight onto the branch the product is built from.
why_it_matters: Work that bypasses pull requests is invisible to every review, approval and audit control the organisation believes it has. This metric measures the size of that blind spot, which means it also bounds how much the review metrics above can be trusted.
how_to_read: Near zero is the goal, and branch protection is what achieves it. A high value means the review numbers describe only part of what is actually shipping.
formula: {direct} landings on {branch} not traceable to a pull request / {landings} = {value}%
assumptions: A landing is credited to a pull request when its commit appears in that pull request's commit list, or when a merge commit references the pull request number.
caveats: Pull requests are fetched newest-first up to the configured page limit, so on very busy repositories the oldest pull requests can fall outside the collected window. The sample figures on this metric state exactly how many were read. | Squash merges rewrite commit hashes, which can make properly reviewed work look like a direct push. Check the named examples before acting on a high figure.

label: Share of branches abandoned over 90 days
plain_english: How many of the parallel lines of work in this repository have had no activity for more than three months. In practice: work that was started and neither finished nor cleaned up.
why_it_matters: Each stale branch is unfinished work somebody was paid for that delivered nothing. In volume it is also a security concern, because old branches keep old vulnerable dependencies — and occasionally old credentials — alive and reachable.
how_to_read: Under 20% is tidy. Over half means nobody is cleaning up, and the total branch count stops being a useful signal of how much parallel work is happening.
formula: {stale} branches idle over 90 days / {total} branches = {value}%
caveats: Long-lived release and environment branches are legitimately old and count as stale unless excluded in configuration. Check the named list before reporting this.

label: Branches
plain_english: A branch is a parallel copy of the code where somebody works without disturbing everyone else. This is how many exist right now.
why_it_matters: Branch count is a rough measure of how much work is in flight simultaneously, and of how much housekeeping is being neglected. Both matter for merge pain.
how_to_read: Read it together with the stale share. Fifty branches of which forty are stale is a cleanup problem; fifty active branches on a ten-person team is a coordination problem.
formula: count(branches on the remote at collection time) = {value}

label: Share of work saved outside working hours
plain_english: The share of saved work recorded before 8am or after 7pm in the author's own recorded time zone. Roughly: how much of the work happens outside a normal working day.
why_it_matters: This is the cheapest early warning of unsustainable pace available, and it usually moves before attrition does. It also acts as a control on the velocity numbers: output that rose alongside this figure was bought with people's evenings, not with efficiency.
how_to_read: Under 15% is normal — everyone has the occasional late night. A sustained rise, especially one that starts at a specific date, is worth a conversation rather than a target. Watch for it moving in step with a deadline or a tool rollout.
formula: {after_hours} commits outside {start}:00-{end}:00 local / {n} commits = {value}%
assumptions: Uses the timezone offset git recorded on each commit, which reflects the machine's clock at the time. This is the author's real local time in almost all cases.
caveats: Commit time is when work was saved, not when it was done. Someone who codes in the afternoon and commits at 9pm looks like a late worker. | Genuinely distributed teams and deliberate flexible schedules both show up as after-hours work. This is a prompt to ask, never a conclusion on its own. | This breaks down by individual. Published research and hard experience both show that per-person delivery metrics change behaviour once people can see themselves ranked. Use it to find where help is needed, not to compare colleagues.

label: Share of work saved at weekends
plain_english: The share of saved work recorded on a Saturday or Sunday. Unlike a late evening, which can be a personal preference, weekend work is usually a response to a deadline that the working week could not absorb.
why_it_matters: Weekend work is the clearest signal that a schedule is not working. Unlike a late evening, it rarely happens by preference, and it correlates strongly with the periods teams later describe as their worst.
how_to_read: Under 5% is background noise. A sustained figure above 15% means the plan depends on weekends, which means the plan is wrong rather than the team being slow.
formula: {weekend} commits on Saturday or Sunday / {n} commits = {value}%
caveats: Assumes a Saturday-Sunday weekend, which is wrong for parts of the world. Configure it per team where that applies. | This breaks down by individual. Published research and hard experience both show that per-person delivery metrics change behaviour once people can see themselves ranked. Use it to find where help is needed, not to compare colleagues.

label: Busiest hour of the day
plain_english: The hour of the day when the most work gets saved, in each author's own local time.
why_it_matters: It shows when the team is actually productive, which is what meeting schedules should be built around. A team whose peak is late afternoon is being interrupted all morning.
how_to_read: Mid-morning or mid-afternoon peaks are typical and healthy. A late-evening peak means the working day is being consumed by something other than the work.
formula: hour with the most commits over {n} commits = {value}
caveats: Rebases, force-pushes and history rewrites change commit hashes and dates. Older history can therefore appear tidier, or more recent, than it actually was.

label: How bursty the work pattern is
plain_english: Whether work arrives in a steady stream or in concentrated bursts. It compares the variability of the gaps between saved checkpoints against their average length. Higher means more feast-and-famine.
why_it_matters: Bursty patterns usually mean people are blocked and then suddenly unblocked, which is a flow problem rather than an effort problem. It is also a documented signature of AI-assisted workflows, where a long exploratory pause is followed by rapid acceptance of several suggestions.
how_to_read: Around 1.0 means gaps vary about as much as their average, which is ordinary. Above 2.0 means strongly bursty. Interpret as a shift over time rather than a level to fix.
formula: standard deviation of inter-commit gaps / mean gap over {n} gaps = {value}
caveats: Holidays, sprint boundaries and release freezes all create bursts that have nothing to do with how anyone works. | Sensitive to the size of the window measured. Compare like-for-like periods only.

label: Share of automated checks that failed
also_known_as: build failure rate | red build rate
plain_english: Every time someone proposes a change, an automated set of checks runs against it. This is the share of those runs that failed.
why_it_matters: A build that frequently fails stops being a signal. Teams learn to ignore it, re-run it, or merge past it — at which point the organisation is paying for a safety net that nobody trusts and that catches nothing.
how_to_read: Ten to twenty percent is healthy: the checks are catching real problems. Above 40% usually means flaky tests rather than bad code, and the fix is to stabilise the tests. Near zero can mean the checks are too shallow to fail.
formula: {failed} failed runs / {n} completed runs = {value}%
caveats: Workflow runs are fetched newest-first up to the configured page limit, so this describes recent pipeline behaviour rather than full history. The sample figures state exactly how many runs were read. | Only visible when the repository uses GitHub Actions. A team using Jenkins, GitLab CI, Azure Pipelines or CircleCI will show nothing here, which is a gap in this tool rather than a finding about the team.

label: Median time for automated checks to finish
plain_english: How long a developer typically waits for the automated checks to finish before they know whether their change is safe.
why_it_matters: This wait is paid on every single change, by every developer, several times a day. It is the highest-leverage number in this report for improving day-to-day productivity, because halving it compounds across every change the team will ever make.
how_to_read: Under 10 minutes keeps people in flow. Beyond 30 minutes developers context-switch away and lose the thread, so the real cost is far higher than the clock time suggests.
formula: median(run duration) over {n} completed runs = {value} minutes
caveats: Workflow runs are fetched newest-first up to the configured page limit, so this describes recent pipeline behaviour rather than full history. The sample figures state exactly how many runs were read. | Only visible when the repository uses GitHub Actions. A team using Jenkins, GitLab CI, Azure Pipelines or CircleCI will show nothing here, which is a gap in this tool rather than a finding about the team. | Includes time spent queued waiting for a runner, which is what the developer actually experiences but is not the same as the pipeline's own execution time.

label: Automated check runs per week
plain_english: How many times per week the automated checks were triggered. Each run is one occasion where the tests, build and quality gates were exercised against somebody's change.
why_it_matters: It shows whether automation is actually in the team's path or bolted on the side. It is also the multiplier on pipeline duration and cost: a slow pipeline run twice a week is a nuisance, run two hundred times a week it is a budget line.
how_to_read: Should be at least as high as the number of changes landing. Much lower means checks are not running on every change.
formula: {n} runs over {weeks} weeks = {value} per week
caveats: Workflow runs are fetched newest-first up to the configured page limit, so this describes recent pipeline behaviour rather than full history. The sample figures state exactly how many runs were read. | Only visible when the repository uses GitHub Actions. A team using Jenkins, GitLab CI, Azure Pipelines or CircleCI will show nothing here, which is a gap in this tool rather than a finding about the team.

label: Share of AI suggestions actually accepted
plain_english: When an AI tool offers a suggestion, the developer either takes it or ignores it. This is the share that was taken, recorded by the tool itself rather than guessed from the change history.
why_it_matters: It is the clearest measure of whether the tools are actually useful to the people holding the licences. A low rate means suggestions are not good enough to accept, which is a training or configuration problem rather than a reason to cancel.
how_to_read: Twenty to thirty percent is the commonly reported band. Very low means the tool is interrupting more than helping. Very high can mean people are accepting without reading, which shows up later as rework.
formula: {accepted} lines accepted / {suggested} lines suggested = {value}%
assumptions: Counted from the export you supplied, over the dates that export covers.
caveats: Covers only the window the tool's telemetry was switched on for. Everything before that date was never recorded and cannot be recovered.

label: Lines accepted from AI suggestions (measured)
plain_english: How many lines of code developers took from AI suggestions, as counted by the tool that made them. Unlike everything else in this section, this is a measurement rather than an inference.
why_it_matters: This is the number people think they are asking for when they ask how much code is AI-written. It is the only figure in the report that can answer it directly, and it only exists for the period the tool was recording.
how_to_read: Compare it against total lines added over the same window to get a real share. Note that accepted does not mean survived — read it next to the rework rate.
formula: sum(accepted lines across {days} days of recorded telemetry) = {value}
caveats: Accepted at the moment of typing. A line accepted and then deleted an hour later still counts here, so this is an upper bound on AI-authored code that survived. | Only covers the dates present in the export.

label: How far the commit-trace floor understates measured AI use
plain_english: This report's main AI figures are a floor, built from signatures that tools optionally leave behind. Where a tool's own records are available for the same period, this compares the two and shows how many times larger the recorded figure is.
why_it_matters: It puts a number on the report's biggest known weakness. If the floor understates real usage threefold, then every historical AI figure in here should be read with that multiplier in mind — and that is a far more useful thing to tell leadership than either figure alone.
how_to_read: A value of 1.0 means the floor was about right; 3.0 means recorded usage was three times the floor. Anything well above 1 is evidence that commit signatures are being suppressed or never emitted, and that the historical trend is understated rather than wrong.
formula: measured share over the covered window ({measured}%) / trace-based floor ({floor}%) = {value}x
assumptions: Both figures are restricted to the dates the export covers, so they describe the same period.
caveats: The two sides count different things: one counts lines accepted at typing time, the other counts lines arriving in commits that carried a signature. The ratio is an indication of scale, not a precise correction factor. | Only computable for the window the tool's telemetry covers.
